title: Mini project: calculator

youtube.title: C++ Mini Project: Build a Calculator | C++ Programming EP 30
youtube.description: In this episode you will split a program into functions, read an expression with cin and choose an operation with switch, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Mini project: calculator · 1:10 The calculator · 2:13 The plan · 2:52 Second program · 4:07 Recap · 4:37 Bug of the Day · 5:35 Challenge · 6:02 Next episode

thumbnail.pose: Xecxec next to a calculator made from code blocks

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we build a mini project. You will join functions, input and switch into a working calculator.

scenes.onScreen: "Mini project: calculator": numbered lines (1. Plan the functions first; 2. One function does one job; 3. main only joins the pieces) and an analogy card: a kitchen with stations: each cook does one job
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: Good programs are made of small functions. Each function does one job. Main only joins them together. Our calculator has three jobs. First, read the numbers and the sign. Second, calculate. Third, print the answer. Think of a kitchen with stations. Each cook does one job. A calculator is a good first project, because it uses most of what you learned. It uses input, decisions, functions and output. Plan first, and then write. Decide the inputs, the steps and the output. Then write one function for each step, and test them one at a time.

analogy.title: Mini project: calculator
analogy.body: A kitchen with stations: each cook does one job

scenes.onScreen: calc.cpp: calc takes two numbers and a sign
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 4] Calc takes two numbers and a sign. [HL 5] A switch picks the operation. [HL 6] Plus adds. [HL 8] Times multiplies. [HL 9] For divide, we first check that b is not zero. [HL 17] Main reads three values with one cin line. [HL 18] It prints the whole sum, and the answer. Twelve times three is thirty-six. [HL 4] The function has three inputs, two numbers and one sign. It gives back one number. [HL 5] A switch is the right tool for one char with many choices. [HL 9] The question mark line is a short if. If b is not zero, it divides. If not, it returns zero. We never divide by zero. [HL 10] The default case catches signs that we do not know.

scenes.onScreen: a flow: read, choose, calculate, print
scenes.animation: Steps drop in left to right with a pop; connecting arrows draw on; the active step glows butter
scenes.narration: Here is the plan. First, cin reads the numbers and the sign. Next, the switch in calc picks the operation. Then calc returns the answer. Last, cout prints the full line. Notice the clear steps. Each step has one owner. Cin reads, calc decides, and cout shows. If the output is wrong, you know where to look first. That is the strength of small functions.

diagram.caption: a flow: read, choose, calculate, print

steps.label: Read
steps.detail: cin reads a, op and b

scenes.onScreen: convert.cpp: two small functions convert units
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 4] This function turns kilometres into miles. [HL 5] This one turns Celsius into Fahrenheit. [HL 8] Ten kilometres is about six point two one miles. [HL 9] Thirty degrees Celsius is eighty-six degrees Fahrenheit. Each function has one small job, so they are easy to test. [HL 4] Each function has one clear job and one clear name. A reader sees the name and knows what it does, without reading the body. [HL 5] The formula for Fahrenheit multiplies by nine, divides by five, and adds thirty-two.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as convert dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints six point two one three seven one, and then eighty-six. Check the second number. Thirty times nine is two hundred seventy, divided by five is fifty-four, plus thirty-two is eighty-six.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. Plan the functions before you write the code. Two. Each function does one job. Three. Main joins the pieces together. Four. Small functions are easy to test. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: Plan the functions before you write the code.
Small functions are easy to test.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: A function that forgets to return
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; the g++ warning appears in tomato; the fix slides in and the warning goes away with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. The calc function handles only plus and minus. For any other sign, it reaches the end with no return. The compiler warns about control reaching the end of a non-void function. Add a final return for every other path. Think about all the paths. A switch has many branches, and each one must return a value. If one path has no return, the function ends with no value, and the answer is garbage. Add a default case, and return something safe.

scenes.onScreen: My calculator and I have a great relationship. We always add up.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: My calculator and I have a great relationship. We always add up.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: add a power option to the calculator
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Add a case for the sign caret in calc. It should return a raised to the power b. Use the pow function. Hint: the pow function lives in the cmath header, so include it at the top. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: We end module three here. Next time: arrays, a row of boxes in memory. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
Compiler output (a warning, the program still builds):

calc.cpp: In function 'double calc(double, char, double)':
calc.cpp:9:1: warning: control reaches end of non-void function [-Wreturn-type]
    9 | }
      | ^
bug.why: If op is neither plus nor minus, the function reaches the end without a return. Every path must return a value.

pun: "My calculator and I have a great relationship. We always add up."
challenge: Add a case for the sign caret in calc. It should return a raised to the power b. Use the pow function. Hint: the pow function lives in the cmath header, so include it at the top.
challengeAnswer: Include cmath. Add case with the caret in single quotes. Return pow of a and b.
